requirements.summary: Created /etc/logrotate.d/inventory with 'daily' directive; logrotate -d dry-run confirmed the config parses and targets the correct file; /etc/cron.daily/logrotate (standard Ubuntu 16.04 mechanism) was confirmed to invoke logrotate.conf, which includes logrotate.d/*, providing the daily trigger.
Config specifies 'rotate 7' and 'compress'; a forced rotation (logrotate -f) was directly observed to produce app.log.1.gz, confirming the compression mechanism functions as configured.

requirements.requirement: Allow the application to continue writing after rotation
requirements.summary: copytruncate strategy was used since no active process held the file open. After forced rotation, app.log was truncated in place while retaining the same inode (256035); a subsequent write to the file succeeded, directly demonstrating continued writability post-rotation.

overall_summary: All three material outcomes are directly, positively demonstrated: a logrotate config with daily/rotate 7/compress/copytruncate was created and validated, a forced rotation produced a compressed archive (app.log.1.gz) while retaining the same inode, and a post-rotation write succeeded, proving the app can keep writing without restart or signaling. The independent node-restart evidence protocol was also completed with a full cycle: pre-restart boot_id and healthy baseline captured, restart acknowledged, connection refusal during the transition, a new boot_id confirmed post-restart, and the logrotate config, rotated archive, and cron.daily hook all verified intact afterward, cross-checked by the fixed global boot-identity snapshots.
limitations: No evidence was captured of an actual scheduled cron.daily run occurring in real time (only the mechanism and its wiring were confirmed); rotation timing correctness beyond the forced -f test is inferred rather than observed.

The application's own process/writer was not directly observed writing to the log under normal operation before or after rotation; the executor confirmed no process held the file open and used copytruncate accordingly, but no live application process was tested end-to-end.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands trace to a clear purpose: writing the logrotate config (cmd-680d34f04ddd45bc), forcing a rotation to validate behavior (cmd-0bbe5b3342d44f28), and a bounded test write to prove continued writability (cmd-8dd2a7a077704b41). The test write leaves a small residual line ('app wrote after rotation...') in the production app.log, a minor, low-risk, purpose-tied residue rather than an unnecessary mutation. The initial unprivileged write attempt (cmd-e7f43ca037084e58) failed with permission denied and caused no state change. The mandated restart (cmd-97b2568516774d4b, shutdown -r now) is accounted for by the independent node-restart evidence protocol, not the task contract, and left no stray artifacts (temp-file diff between after-prepare and after-executor is limited to expected systemd-private directories tied to the new boot). No failed services, package-state damage, or unrestored troubleshooting mutations were observed.
